name: Shinto
idea: Shinto has no founder, no single scripture, and little formal ethical doctrine, and it does not teach that life is a test. Its core concerns are kami, ritual purity, gratitude, and the harmony of the community; the old chronicles are mythic and historical records, not moral codes. Related ideas appear around the edges: purification after wrongdoing or pollution, makoto (sincerity or genuineness, a value with Shinto associations), and harmony among neighbors.

passages.text: it is meet that I should cleanse my body from its pollutions.
passages.ref: Nihongi, Book I (Age of the Gods), Izanagi after Yomi
passages.translation: W. G. Aston, Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, 1896

passages.text: But when those above are harmonious and those below are friendly, and there is concord in the discussion of business, right views of things spontaneously gain acceptance.
passages.ref: Nihongi, Book XXII (Suiko), Constitution of Prince Shotoku, article I
passages.translation: W. G. Aston, Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, 1896

passages.text: When Heaven establishes a Prince, it is for the sake of the people. The Prince must therefore make the people the foundation.
passages.translation: W. G. Aston, Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, 1896

practices.how: Rinse your hands and mouth, as at a shrine basin, before an important task, and take a quiet moment to begin fresh.
Sweep a stairwell, sidewalk, or common room that is not yours alone. Communities traditionally keep shrine grounds clean together.
Practice makoto this week: keep one small promise exactly, and avoid saying what you do not mean.
Offer a hand at a local festival, cleanup, or gathering so community harmony is built by work and not only by wishes.
Before a meal or at a place you love, pause in gratitude to the unseen powers and people who made it possible.

ask: How does our shrine or priest teach makoto in dealings with strangers and with people who cannot repay us?
How do we understand the kami's regard for us, as watching our conduct, or as presences to be honored and thanked?
What does purification mean in our practice, ritual cleansing only, or also making amends for wrongdoing?
caveat: Shinto is diverse (shrine, folk, and sectarian forms, and a modern history of State Shinto), and many people practice it alongside Buddhism. The passages here come from 8th-century chronicles whose later parts show Chinese and Buddhist influence, so this guide offers resonance only and does not claim Shinto teaches that life is a test.
